questions.stem: An HR team of six people uses Claude to answer new-hire questions. Each person starts a fresh chat and pastes the same 40-page employee handbook and benefits summary every time, and the team keeps hitting usage limits by midweek. Which change would MOST improve efficiency without lowering the quality of the answers?

options.text: Switch everyone to the most capable model so that fewer follow-up questions are needed per chat.
Create a shared Project holding the handbook and benefits summary as knowledge, with instructions on tone and escalation.
Paste only the first few pages of the handbook into each chat so that every message is shorter.
Have each person keep one very long chat open all quarter so the handbook never needs to be pasted again.

questions.explanation: The waste is **repetition**: the same 40 pages are pasted into every new chat. A shared Project stores the handbook and benefits summary once as project knowledge, and its standing instructions keep tone and escalation consistent for all six people. Configuring Projects with instructions and knowledge sources is a core Associate skill (exam guide Domains 3 and 5), and it eliminates the redundant re-uploads that burn through the team's weekly allowance.

whyWrong.A: A more capable model is matched to complex reasoning, not routine handbook Q&A, and it does nothing about the actual source of the waste: the same documents being pasted into every chat.
whyWrong.C: This saves usage by removing the information Claude needs. Answers about benefits or later handbook sections would become guesses, so quality drops.
whyWrong.D: One ever-growing chat carries the whole history into every new message. The exam guide's context-limitation objective (when to restart, summarize, or persist) exists because long conversations get costlier and lose early details; static reference material belongs in Project knowledge, not a months-long chat.

questions.mindset: Store material you reuse once (Project knowledge) instead of pasting it into every chat.

questions.scenario: A contracts team redesigned its Claude workflow for first-draft NDAs. They moved to a lighter model and removed the approved example NDAs from the Project to shorten the context. Drafting now takes about 10 minutes instead of 40. Over the same month, the share of drafts that legal reviewers send back for a second round rose from 15% to 45%.
questions.stem: The team lead wants to report the redesign to leadership as a successful optimization. What is the MOST appropriate assessment and next step?

options.text: Report it as a success, because drafting time fell by 75% and speed was the main goal of the redesign.
Revert every change at once and go back to the original workflow until a completely new plan is approved.
Keep the faster setup and add a step where Claude reviews each draft for errors before it goes to legal.
Count total time including rework, restore one change at a time (examples first), and re-measure after each.

questions.explanation: An optimization must improve efficiency **without hurting effectiveness**. Tripling the send-back rate means the time saved in drafting is likely lost again in rework, so the honest measure is total time to an approved draft. The removed examples are the most likely cause of the drop, so restore changes one at a time and re-measure: that isolates the cause (the lighter model may be fine once the examples are back) and keeps any gain that was real. This mirrors the docs' guidance to get quality right first, then optimize for speed.

whyWrong.A: This judges the change on one number and ignores the rework it caused. A faster draft that legal rejects three times as often is not a real optimization.
whyWrong.B: Reverting everything at once throws away any gain that was real and teaches nothing about which change caused the drop. Changing one thing at a time does both.
whyWrong.C: Claude reviewing its own drafts is not an independent check — self-assessment is not a reliable accuracy signal — and it adds a step without fixing the likely cause.

questions.mindset: Faster but worse is not optimized; measure total time including rework and change one variable at a time.

questions.stem: An event coordinator needs Claude to tighten 12 conference session abstracts to 80 words each in the company's house style. Today she opens a separate chat for each abstract and retypes the style rules each time, and the results vary from abstract to abstract. She repeats this task before every quarterly event. Which TWO changes would BEST improve both efficiency and consistency? Choose TWO.

options.text: Send all 12 abstracts in one message with one complete set of style rules and the 80-word limit.
Keep a separate chat for each abstract so that every abstract gets Claude's full attention.
Switch to the most capable model for every one of the abstracts.
Store the house style rules and one approved example abstract in a Project she uses for each event.
Ask Claude after every abstract whether it fully followed the house style before moving on.

questions.explanation: Two separate fixes. **Sending all 12 abstracts in one complete request** applies the same rules to every abstract at once, which removes the retyping and the drift between separate chats. **Storing the house style and an approved example in a Project** makes the setup reusable every quarter — and concrete examples are the most reliable way to enforce a consistent format; the prompting docs describe examples as more effective than abstract instructions for exactly this purpose.

whyWrong.B: Separate chats are what cause the retyping and the variation. Claude can handle 12 short abstracts in one message without losing quality.
whyWrong.C: Tightening an abstract is a simple, well-defined task. A more capable model uses the team's allowance faster and does nothing about the retyped, inconsistent rules — the actual cause of the variation.
whyWrong.E: Asking Claude to grade its own compliance adds a message per abstract and is not a reliable check. A clear rule set and an example prevent the problem in the first place.

questions.mindset: Apply one complete request to similar items, and keep recurring rules in a reusable place with an example.

questions.stem: A finance operations analyst has a precise nine-step procedure for turning raw vendor data into a quarterly scorecard in the company template. Colleagues on several teams, each working in their own Projects, now want to run the same procedure. Copying the steps into every Project has led to different versions drifting apart. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Add all nine steps to each colleague's default instructions so they apply in every chat that colleague opens.
Email the latest procedure each quarter as a document and ask colleagues to paste it into their chats.
Package the procedure and template as one Skill colleagues use, so Claude loads it when a scorecard is requested.
Ask an architect to design a dedicated agent system that builds the scorecards automatically end to end.

questions.explanation: A **Skill** packages instructions and supporting resources (such as the template) for a specific, repeatable task, and Claude loads it when that task comes up, so the procedure is available wherever a scorecard is needed without filling every other chat. Keeping one packaged version also ends the drift caused by copying the steps into many Projects. Skills are among the platform features the exam guide expects Associates to know and select appropriately.

whyWrong.A: Default instructions apply to every conversation, including ones that have nothing to do with scorecards. Each colleague would also still hold a separate copy that can drift.
whyWrong.B: This keeps the manual pasting and the version drift. Someone will paste last quarter's copy.
whyWrong.D: The problem is sharing a known procedure, which a built-in feature handles. Commissioning an agent system is over-engineering for this need.

questions.mindset: A repeatable, specialized procedure belongs in a Skill, not copied into every chat or Project.

questions.stem: A marketing assistant turns on Research for every request, including quick rewrites of a single paragraph and one-line definitions of terms. Responses take much longer than expected, and the team's usage runs out early in the week. What should the assistant do?

options.text: Use regular chat for quick, self-contained tasks and keep Research for multi-source investigations needing citations.
Keep Research on for every request, but make each request shorter so the research finishes more quickly.
Turn Research off permanently, because its citations are not reliable enough for marketing work.
Switch to a lighter model but keep Research turned on for every request, including the short rewrites.

questions.explanation: Match the feature to the job. Research mode searches across many sources and returns a cited report — valuable for a real investigation, and slow, costly overkill for rewriting a paragraph or defining a term. Selecting the right product feature (chat vs. research mode) is a Domain 3 skill, and the team's usage lasts longer when heavy features run only for tasks that actually need them.

whyWrong.B: Shorter requests do not change the fact that Research is the wrong tool for a paragraph rewrite. The tool is still running searches the task does not need.
whyWrong.C: This overreacts. Research is the right choice for multi-source questions, and its citations can be checked. The problem is when it is used, not that it exists.
whyWrong.D: Changing the model leaves the main waste — unnecessary Research on trivial tasks — in place.

questions.mindset: Use the lightest feature that does the job; save heavy tools for tasks that need them.

questions.scenario: A consultant asks Claude to write a complete 25-page client proposal in a single request. After reading it, the engagement partner rejects the structure: the client wanted phased options, not one plan. Most sections have to be rewritten. The same thing has happened on two previous proposals.
questions.stem: Which workflow change would MOST reduce wasted effort on future proposals?

options.text: Ask Claude to produce two complete 25-page versions every time so the partner can choose one of them.
Have Claude draft an outline of the structure, get the partner's approval, then draft section by section.
Add "make sure the structure matches what the client wants" to the end of each proposal request.
Switch to the most capable model so that the first full draft is more likely to be correct.

questions.explanation: The costly error is in the **structure**, and it is found only after 25 pages exist. Decomposing the task — outline first, partner approval, then section-by-section drafting — puts a cheap checkpoint before the expensive work, so a wrong structure costs minutes to fix instead of a full rewrite. Inspecting intermediate output before continuing is exactly what task decomposition and chained steps are for, and the exam guide lists decomposition as a core prompting skill.

whyWrong.A: Doubling the output doubles the cost and still guesses at the structure. Both versions may miss what the client asked for.
whyWrong.C: Claude does not know what the client wants unless someone tells it. This adds words, not information, and still puts the check at the end.
whyWrong.D: The issue is missing direction from the partner, not model capability. A stronger model still writes the full document before anyone reviews it.

questions.mindset: Put a cheap checkpoint before expensive work: approve the outline before drafting.

questions.scenario: A communications department requires every Claude output to go through a two-day legal review. This includes internal brainstorm lists, meeting-note summaries and press releases. Staff have started avoiding Claude because of the delays, and the legal team is overloaded.
questions.stem: The department head asks for a change that improves throughput without increasing risk. What is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Tier review by risk: author checks for internal drafts, and keep legal review for external or regulated content.
Remove legal review for all content, since Claude's outputs have been reliable for the past several months.
Keep the current policy but have Claude add a notice to every output saying it may contain errors.
Have Claude review its own outputs first so that legal only needs to skim each item before approving.

questions.explanation: Review effort should match the cost of an error. A brainstorm list read by three colleagues does not need the same check as a press release. Deciding **when human review or additional verification is required** — a named Domain 2 objective — means keeping expert review where mistakes are costly (external, regulated, legal content) and using lighter author checks elsewhere. That frees legal capacity and speeds internal work while oversight stays where it matters.

whyWrong.B: Past reliability does not guarantee future accuracy. Models can still produce confident errors — the docs are explicit that safeguards reduce but do not eliminate them — and press releases carry real legal and reputational risk.
whyWrong.C: A disclaimer neither speeds anything up nor reduces risk. Every item still waits two days.
whyWrong.D: Claude checking itself is not an independent check, and self-assessment is not a reliable accuracy signal. Legal would be skimming high-risk content it should still read carefully.

questions.mindset: Put human review where errors are costly, not everywhere equally.

questions.stem: A sales team uses a shared Project to draft client proposals. Some reps paste detailed notes on budget, timeline and decision-makers; others send one line such as "proposal for Acme." Quality varies widely, and the weak proposals need several rounds of revision. Which change would MOST improve the workflow?

options.text: Upgrade the Project to the most capable model so that it can infer the missing client details on its own.
Add a Project instruction telling Claude never to produce a weak or generic proposal for any client.
Introduce a short intake template (goal, budget, timeline, decision-makers) that reps fill in before asking.
Let Claude fill any gaps with typical industry figures and flag them so reps can check them later on.

questions.explanation: The variation comes from the **inputs**, not from Claude. A short intake template standardizes what goes in — goal, budget, timeline, decision-makers — so every request starts from the same quality of context. Clear, complete context is the foundation of good output: consistent inputs are what produce consistent proposals and cut the revision rounds.

whyWrong.A: No model can know a client's budget or decision-makers if nobody provides them. A more capable model just writes more convincing guesses.
whyWrong.B: An instruction to "not be weak" adds no information. Without the client details, Claude still has nothing specific to work with — vague directives do not change what the model can know.
whyWrong.D: This puts invented figures into client documents and moves the work to a later check that is easy to miss. It raises risk instead of fixing the input.

questions.mindset: Consistent inputs produce consistent outputs: standardize the brief.

questions.stem: A program manager on a paid Claude plan starts each week's planning chat by typing out a long summary of the decisions made in last week's chats. This takes about 15 minutes and the summary is often incomplete. Searching past chats is enabled on her account. Which approach is MOST efficient?

options.text: Keep all planning in one chat that grows every week so nothing ever has to be re-explained.
Upload every past chat transcript as a new file at the start of each week's planning chat.
Switch to a more capable model that can recall last week's decisions without being reminded.
Ask Claude to search her previous chats for last week's decisions and confirm them before planning.

questions.explanation: The stem establishes that past-chat search is enabled on her account. Asking Claude to retrieve last week's decisions replaces 15 minutes of incomplete retyping, and confirming the retrieved list before planning catches anything missed or misread. Managing what carries across sessions — when to restart, summarize, or persist — is exactly the context and memory consideration the exam guide's Domain 3 describes.

whyWrong.A: A chat that grows every week carries the full history into each new message, so it uses the plan's allowance faster and early details get progressively harder to keep straight.
whyWrong.B: Re-uploading whole transcripts every week adds large, repeated attachments and buries the decisions in noise.
whyWrong.C: Model choice does not give Claude access to other conversations. A more capable model is not a retrieval feature.

questions.mindset: Refer back to earlier work with built-in search instead of retyping it.

questions.scenario: A policy analyst has worked for three weeks in a single chat analyzing eight long regional reports, re-attaching some of them whenever Claude seems to lose track. Responses are slower, earlier conclusions are sometimes contradicted, and she hits her usage limit most afternoons.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would BEST reduce usage while keeping or improving answer quality? Choose TWO.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model for every message she sends.
Ask Claude for a summary of conclusions and open questions, then continue in a fresh chat using it.
Split each question into several short messages so that every individual message uses less.
Re-attach all eight reports at the start of every message so that none of them are forgotten.
Move the eight reports into a Project's knowledge so they are reused rather than uploaded again.

questions.explanation: The two cost drivers named in the stem are a very long conversation and repeated large attachments. **Summarize and restart**: asking Claude to summarize conclusions and open questions, then continuing in a fresh chat, removes three weeks of history from every message and puts the agreed conclusions up front — the exam guide's context objective explicitly covers knowing when to restart or summarize, and it also stops the contradictions from a bloated history. **Project knowledge** holds the eight reports once so they stop being re-attached message after message.

whyWrong.A: A more capable model uses the plan's allowance faster and leaves both real drivers — the long history and the repeated attachments — untouched.
whyWrong.C: More messages means more back-and-forth, and each one is still processed with the full three-week history. Neither driver is removed.
whyWrong.D: Repeated large attachments are already a main driver of the usage problem. This adds even more weight to every message.

questions.mindset: Long histories and repeated uploads are the hidden costs; reset with a summary and store documents once.

questions.stem: A customer-success lead is about to roll out a new Claude workflow for drafting renewal emails. A month later she must show leadership whether the change was a real optimization. Which TWO measures, recorded both before and after the change, would give the MOST meaningful evidence? Choose TWO.

options.text: Average time from the first request to a send-ready renewal email.
Average word count of the renewal emails that Claude produces.
Share of emails a manager sends back for another round of edits.
How confident Claude says it is about each email it writes.
Number of saved prompts added to the team's prompt library.

questions.explanation: A real optimization improves **efficiency** without hurting **effectiveness**, so measure both against a baseline. Time from first request to a send-ready email captures efficiency, including any back-and-forth. The send-back rate captures quality as judged by the person who approves the work. Both are specific, measurable success criteria of the kind the testing docs require — and measuring before and after is what makes the comparison fair.

whyWrong.B: Length says nothing about whether the email worked or how long it took. A shorter email could be worse.
whyWrong.D: Claude's stated confidence is not a reliable signal of accuracy or quality — the exam guide's own sample-question rationale rules out self-reported confidence as a validation step — so it cannot serve as evidence of improvement.
whyWrong.E: This counts activity, not results. A larger library may even slow people down.

questions.mindset: Prove an optimization with before-and-after measures of both speed and quality.

questions.scenario: An operations lead at a logistics firm wants a daily summary of overnight support tickets. The tickets live in an internal ticketing system that has no connector available in her Claude workspace, though it does allow a bulk export. Each morning she copies tickets by hand into a chat, which takes about 45 minutes.
questions.stem: She would like the summary to be produced automatically every night with nobody in the chat. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate for her as an Associate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Write a detailed prompt instructing Claude to check the ticketing system on its own every night.
Cut the manual step now by using the bulk export and a Project whose instructions define the summary format.
Find a third-party script online and connect it to the ticketing system herself this week.
Escalate the automation need to developers or architects, with sample tickets and the target format.
Switch to the most capable model so that Claude can reach the ticketing system directly.

questions.explanation: Unattended, scheduled automation that reads from an unconnected internal system is an integration build — work the exam guide assigns to Claude Developers and Architects, not Associates. The Associate's job is to keep the work moving: cut the 45 minutes now with what the platform already offers (the bulk export plus a Project that holds the summary format and instructions), and hand off the automation request with concrete requirements and examples so the builders do not start from scratch.

whyWrong.A: No wording gives Claude access to a system it is not connected to, or makes a chat run on a schedule. This is a capability gap, not a prompt gap.
whyWrong.C: Connecting unvetted code to an internal system bypasses security and IT review, and building integrations is outside the Associate role.
whyWrong.E: Model choice does not grant access to systems. Connection comes from connectors or integrations, not from a more capable model.

questions.mindset: Optimize what you can with built-in features now; escalate builds with clear requirements.

questions.scenario: To save usage, a strategy team moved all of its Claude work to a lighter model. Most routine tasks are fine. However, the quarterly competitive synthesis, which combines ten long analyst reports into recommendations with trade-offs, now comes back shallow. The team has confirmed that the reports are attached, the instructions are clear, and an approved example sits in the Project.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate adjustment?

options.text: Use a more capable model for the quarterly synthesis only, and keep the lighter model for routine tasks.
Move every task back to the most capable model, since the lighter model has now proven unreliable.
Add several more example syntheses to the Project and keep using the lighter model for this task.
Split the synthesis into ten separate chats, one per report, and paste the ten results together.

questions.explanation: The team has ruled out missing context, vague instructions, and a missing example, so the remaining cause is **capability**. Complex multi-document reasoning with trade-offs is what the most capable models are for: the exam guide's own sample frames the choice as faster, lower-cost models for straightforward high-volume work while reserving the most capable model for complex reasoning. The efficient fix is targeted — move up only for the synthesis and keep the lighter model where it already meets the bar.

whyWrong.B: Routine tasks are already fine on the lighter model. Moving everything up wastes usage to fix one task.
whyWrong.C: An approved example is already there. More examples help with format and style, but they do not add the reasoning depth that trade-off analysis across ten reports needs.
whyWrong.D: Analyzing reports separately loses the comparisons across sources that the synthesis depends on, and pasting the parts together adds manual work.

questions.mindset: Start light and move up only for the tasks that truly need more capability.

questions.stem: A support team's shared prompt library has grown to 35 saved prompts for customer apology emails. Many are near-duplicates written by different people. New hires don't know which to use, and the tone varies noticeably across replies. What is the MOST effective way to optimize this?

options.text: Keep all 35 prompts and add a short note to each one explaining when it works best.
Test the main variants on real past cases, keep the best as one standard template, and retire the rest.
Let each agent write their own prompt from scratch, since personal prompts usually work best.
Ask Claude to merge all 35 prompts into one very long prompt that covers every possible case.

questions.explanation: Near-duplicate prompts create the very inconsistency they were meant to prevent. Comparing the main candidates on **real past cases** — the docs' guidance is to test against realistic examples — shows which one actually performs best. Making that the single standard template gives consistent tone and a clear starting point for new hires. Variants can come back later if testing shows a real need.

whyWrong.A: Notes keep the clutter and the inconsistency. New hires still face 35 choices, and nothing shows which prompts actually work.
whyWrong.C: This increases variation, which is the problem, and wastes each agent's time rebuilding something the team already has.
whyWrong.D: A merged mega-prompt is likely to contain conflicting instructions, and nobody has tested whether it works better than the best existing prompt.

questions.mindset: Consolidate on the version that tests best on real cases.

questions.stem: A training lead is building an onboarding checklist with Claude that she will refine over several weeks and share with colleagues. Each time, she copies Claude's long chat reply into a separate document by hand and loses track of which version is current. Which approach would MOST improve this workflow?

options.text: Turn on Research so that each new version of the checklist is backed by up-to-date sources.
Ask Claude to repeat the full checklist at the end of every reply so it is always visible in the chat.
Have Claude create the checklist as an artifact she can keep refining in conversation and then share.
Start a new chat for every revision so that each version of the checklist stays in its own place.

questions.explanation: Artifacts are the platform's format for content you create, keep refining, and share — documents, checklists, trackers. A checklist artifact gives her one current version she can refine through conversation or edit directly and then share, ending both the manual copying and the version confusion. Selecting the appropriate output format (artifact vs. inline chat text) is a named Domain 2 objective, and artifacts are among the features the exam guide expects Associates to know.

whyWrong.A: Research is for multi-source investigation. It does nothing about copying and version control, and it uses limits faster.
whyWrong.B: Repeating the whole checklist in every reply makes the conversation longer and costlier, and she still has to copy it out by hand.
whyWrong.D: Scattering versions across many chats makes it harder to know which one is current. That is the very problem she has now.

questions.mindset: Pick the feature built for the output: a living, shareable document belongs in an artifact.
